semantic_fragments.content: The Usability Evaluation Plan, detailing how usability will be assessed, can be included within the verification and validation plan of the overall product realization process. This integration ensures that usability evaluation aligns with broader testing efforts.

Analyses of known use problems and foreseeable use errors become part of the Risk Management File. This integration ensures that risks associated with use errors are managed in alignment with risk management processes.

Tailoring the usability engineering effort for a Infrared Forehead Thermometer is essential to address the specific risks and complexities associated with its use. The level of effort required for usability engineering can vary significantly depending on the nature of the device, its functions, and potential risks. Several considerations should guide the tailoring process: Risk Assessment and Severity, Device Complexity, Novelty, Modification and Change, Previous Records, User Research and Testing, Summative Evaluation, Iterative Process, Usability Engineering Plan.

Begin by assessing the potential risks associated with the Infrared Forehead Thermometer's usability. Focus on identifying hazards and their potential causes that could lead to harm. Consider the severity of potential harm when determining the scope of usability engineering efforts. High-severity risks should receive greater attention.

For novel devices lacking post-production data, prioritize the severity of potential harm over estimating occurrence probability. This approach helps tailor usability engineering efforts to address worst-case scenarios and focuses on minimizing harm.

When modifying an existing user interface, focus on the changed elements and their effects on device use. If unchanged elements remain unaffected, additional usability engineering effort might not be needed. Changes that do not impact the user interface or use specifications might not necessitate additional effort.

Tailor the extent of user research and testing based on device complexity and risks. Research efforts might involve a smaller or larger number of participants. The usability testing scope could vary from involving a comprehensive set of users to specific user groups with distinct responsibilities.

Tailor the quantity and complexity of summative evaluations based on the risk assessment. For some cases, a single usability test with a single user group might suffice to assess hazard-related use scenarios. In other instances, multiple sessions with different user groups might be necessary to assess various scenarios. Good usability engineering practice involves iterative evaluations. If initial summative evaluations indicate modifications are needed, focus subsequent evaluations on those specific elements of the user interface affected by the changes.

The Wireless No-Touch Forehead Thermometer is intended for the intermittent measurement of body temperature from the forehead on people of all ages. It can be used by consumers in the household environment and by healthcare providers.

The Infrared Forehead Thermometer is suitable for people of all ages, including lay persons and professionals. Intended part of the body: Aim the thermometer probe at the center of the forehead and keep the probe 1.18 in (3cm) away from the forehead (the optimal distance is about the width of an adult's index finger).

Intended USER PROFILE: (1) Experience: minimum: no special experience needed; no maximum. (2) Age: people of all ages. (3) Education: several years of intensive reading experience (school); no maximum.
